part_title: CloudFront Origin Failover, Geography and Price Class Decisions

scenes.title: Origin group failover contract
scenes.visual_overview: Primary/secondary origin group; configured status codes and connection timeout; only GET/HEAD and cached OPTIONS eligible.
visual_walkthrough: Trace cache miss to primary origin and examine eligible failure responses or connection errors
Show retry to the secondary origin for qualifying safe request methods
Explain why origin group failover is a per-request decision rather than a persistent active-region switch
scenes.visual_example: A GET for a static asset fails at the primary origin and can be attempted at a secondary origin, while an application POST is not handled by the same origin-group failover behavior.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Do not claim CloudFront origin groups provide continuous health checks or automatic failover for every HTTP method.
scenes.narration: This failure sequence follows a CloudFront origin group. A request that requires an origin fetch is first sent to the configured primary origin. When a qualifying error status or connection failure occurs, CloudFront can retry the request using the secondary origin. The inset is crucial: origin-group failover applies to eligible GET and HEAD requests and supported OPTIONS behavior, not arbitrary state-changing POST or PUT operations. The configured error statuses and timeouts determine the exact failover contract. This is not a permanent regional promotion, a weighted origin policy or a health-check dashboard that continuously marks one origin as down. Imagine a static download served by two origin backends. A failed eligible read can be retried on the secondary path, while a failed purchase submission needs application-level transaction handling. Design caching, data consistency and failover together rather than assuming an origin group provides full disaster recovery.

scenes.title: CloudFront geographic restrictions
scenes.visual_overview: Distribution country allowlist/blocklist uses GeoIP; distinguish coarse content restriction from robust user authorization.
visual_walkthrough: Read the map-style allowed and blocked country regions as coarse geographic policy
Trace a viewer request through GeoIP-based country evaluation
Distinguish distribution geographic restrictions from identity, entitlement and licensing enforcement
scenes.visual_example: A publisher blocks content delivery from selected countries but still authenticates paying subscribers individually.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A country-based rule alone does not prove a user's identity or contractual entitlement.
scenes.narration: This map-style slide describes CloudFront geographic restrictions. A distribution can allow or block access based on a viewer's detected country, using IP geolocation to make the policy decision. Follow a viewer request: CloudFront checks the configured geographic restriction and may deny the request before origin processing. The visual distinction is between countries marked eligible and countries marked restricted. This approach can support coarse delivery policies, but IP location is not guaranteed proof of citizenship, residence or content license. It also does not authenticate an individual user. A subscription video service may use a geographic restriction for territory controls while separately enforcing user login, subscription status and application-level authorization. Design legal and commercial enforcement with these limitations in mind. CloudFront geographic restriction answers a country-level routing policy question; it is not a complete entitlement service.

scenes.title: Price class and delivery-cost choices
scenes.visual_overview: Price Class All, 200, 100 trade edge coverage and potential latency for cost; data transfer/request prices vary by geography and commitment.
visual_walkthrough: Compare Price Class All, 200 and 100 as different sets of edge locations
Explain the relationship between audience geography, latency and delivery charges
Avoid presenting fixed prices as universal rates; analyze actual traffic distribution
scenes.visual_example: A predominantly North American and European audience may evaluate a restricted price class, but distant viewer latency can worsen.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Price class alters available delivery edge locations; model cost and performance for the real audience.
scenes.narration: This pricing comparison asks how much global edge coverage an application needs. CloudFront Price Class All provides the widest supported serving edge footprint, while Price Classes 200 and 100 restrict the eligible edge locations to particular geographic sets. Compare the columns as a cost-versus-reach decision, not a guarantee that a smaller class is always better. The map-style inset helps explain why viewer location matters. A site with mainly North American and European traffic might evaluate a restricted class, but visitors elsewhere may experience different request paths or latency. Data transfer rates, requests, traffic geography and any commercial pricing arrangement affect the actual bill. Rather than copying fixed historical prices into an architecture, estimate the distribution of users and data delivered, test application performance and assess the price class against business expectations. Saving on serving edges is useful only when the resulting delivery experience remains acceptable.
